summary: Defines two new flags in the IOAM Trace Option headers, the Loopback and Active flags. In situ OAM collects operational and telemetry information in packets as they traverse a path, and these flags add new ways to use it. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Packets can collect notes about their journey. One new flag asks for a copy to be sent straight back, and another marks a packet as a test one.

questions: what is the ioam loopback flag

subtitle: Two new IOAM flags: one asks every hop to send a trimmed copy of the packet back, the other marks a packet as a measurement probe.

tldr.problem: IOAM lets packets collect telemetry on their way across a network, but there was no way to ask each hop to report back right away, or to mark a packet as a synthetic probe that should not be delivered.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9322 defines two flags in the IOAM Pre-allocated and Incremental Trace options. The Loopback flag makes each transit node send a truncated copy of the packet back to the sender. The Active flag tells the decapsulating node to terminate the packet.
tldr.outcome: Operators get a faster alternative to Traceroute and a clear marker for active measurement packets, with rate limits that keep the extra traffic small.

facts.label: Rate limit
facts.value: SHOULD NOT exceed 1/N of interface capacity

today: RFC 9322 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2022. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the IOAM data fields defined in RFC 9197.

sections.title: What the Two Flags Add
sections.content:
IOAM (In situ Operations, Administration, and Maintenance, defined in RFC 9197) monitors traffic by placing IOAM data fields into packets that are already in flight. The data can be carried in one of four options: Pre-allocated Trace, Incremental Trace, Proof of Transit (POT) and Edge-to-Edge.

This document defines two new flags in the Pre-allocated and Incremental Trace options. The Loopback flag asks each transit device on the path to loop back a truncated copy of the data packet to the sender. The Active flag marks a packet as used for active measurement, in the sense of RFC 7799.
sections.eli5: Packets can already carry travel notes. This RFC adds two switches: one that asks for a copy to be mailed back, and one that says the packet is just a test.

sections.title: The New Trace Option Flags
sections.content:
Both flags live in the flag bits of the IOAM Trace options. Bit 0 is the most significant bit and was already allocated by RFC 9197 as the Overflow bit.

  • Bit 1, Loopback (L-bit): when set, triggers sending a copy of the packet back towards the source.
  • Bit 2, Active (A-bit): when set, says the packet is an active measurement packet rather than a data packet. It may be an IOAM probe packet or a replicated data packet.
sections.eli5: Think of two little switches on a packet. Switch one means 'send a copy home'. Switch two means 'I am a practice packet'.

sections.title: How Loopback Works
sections.content:
Loopback lets an IOAM encapsulating node trace the path to a destination and get per-hop data about both the forward and the return path. It is meant as an accelerated alternative to Traceroute: responses from several transit nodes arrive in less than one round-trip time (RTT), and the sender only transmits a single packet.

The encapsulating node either generates synthetic packets with the Loopback flag set or sets the flag on a subset of in-transit data packets, proactively or on demand when a failure is detected. Each transit node and the decapsulating node copies the packet and sends the copy to the source address found in the encapsulation header. The copy is truncated: any payload after the IOAM options is removed. The original packet carries on to its destination, and the L-bit MUST be cleared in the copy.

Loopback only works when the identity of the encapsulating node is in the encapsulation header and a return path exists. On the way back the copy is processed like any other packet with IOAM data, so transit nodes can add data again if there is space.

When a looped-back packet reaches the encapsulating node, the node recognizes it by checking the Node ID in the Hop_Lim/node_id field of the first hop. If the Node ID and IOAM-Namespace match, the node processes it as its own looped-back packet. If another boundary node receives it, the IOAM encapsulation is removed and the payload-free packet is terminated, so IOAM information does not leak out of the IOAM-Domain.
sections.eli5: It is like shouting 'echo!' down a hallway. Every person you pass sends back a short postcard saying 'I was here', while your real letter keeps going to its destination.

sections.title: Limits That Keep Loopback Safe
sections.content:
A packet with the Loopback flag must carry a trace type with the most significant bit of IOAM-Trace-Type set to 1 and all other bits 0. Each transit node then adds only one data field, the Hop_Lim and node_id. A transit node that sees any other trace type MUST NOT loop back a copy. The reason given is to minimize the impact of amplification attacks.

An encapsulating node MUST NOT push an IOAM encapsulation with the Loopback flag onto packets that already include an IOAM encapsulation, which prevents nested loopback.

An encapsulating node MUST be able to apply the flag to a subset of packets. The traffic with the flag SHOULD NOT exceed 1/N of the interface capacity on any interface, where N is operator-configurable. If the number of transit nodes on any path is bounded by M, then N much greater than M is RECOMMENDED, and a default of N greater than 100 is RECOMMENDED when nothing else is known. Nodes that process loopback MUST be able to limit the rate of looped-back packets, and the looped-back data rate SHOULD NOT exceed 1/N of interface capacity.

A domain that uses Loopback MUST be configured so that a return path is expected from every transit and decapsulating node. Otherwise, or if the encapsulating node's identity is not in the header, configuration MUST NOT enable the flag.
sections.eli5: If everyone sent echoes all the time, the hallway would be jammed. So only a few packets get the echo switch, and each helper only writes one short line on its postcard.

sections.title: Active Measurement and the Active Flag
sections.content:
Active measurement uses synthetic packets to make measurements. A decapsulating node that receives a packet with the Active flag set in one of its Trace options must terminate it. This simplifies decapsulating nodes, because the packet should not be forwarded further. The flag is not a replacement for existing active OAM protocols, which may run in higher layers and use the flag.

The RFC describes three use cases:

  • Endpoint active measurement: probes between the source and destination are treated as ordinary data by the IOAM-Domain, and the Active flag is not used.
  • Probe packets within the IOAM-Domain: the encapsulating node generates probes with the Active flag set, and the decapsulating node terminates them. IOAM data may be exported by some other protocol.
  • Replicated data packets: the encapsulating node copies some or all data packets. The replica carries IOAM options with the Active flag set, while the original is forwarded normally without IOAM options. The replica should follow the same path as far as possible.

The details of probe generation, replication and decapsulating-node handling are outside the scope of this document. Traffic with the Active flag SHOULD NOT exceed 1/N of interface capacity on any interface, and N greater than 100 is RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: A practice packet is wearing a sticker that says 'test only'. When it reaches the last stop, the stop sees the sticker and does not deliver it.

sections.title: Performance and Security
sections.content:
Loopback generates more traffic than the endpoints sent, and active measurement needs synthetic overhead traffic. So it MUST be possible to use each mechanism on a subset of traffic, and nodes need rate limits.

IOAM is assumed to be deployed in a restricted administrative domain, which limits the threats. Still, an attacker could inject synthetic packets with the flags, or an on-path attacker could set them on transit packets. Setting the Loopback flag can cause amplification, since every device on the path sends a copy back, and many devices sending to a single source could be used for a DDoS attack. Setting the Active flag on en route packets can keep them from reaching their destination, though an on-path attacker could do the same by changing the destination address. Nested IOAM-Domains that both use loopback could make amplification worse.

The mitigations are the single data field per hop, the truncation of the payload, and the rate limits on Loopback packets, looped-back packets and Active packets.
sections.eli5: Someone naughty could flip the echo switch on lots of packets so a victim gets buried in postcards. That is why helpers write only one line, keep copies short and limit how many they send.

sections.title: IANA Allocations
sections.content: IANA allocated two bits in the IOAM Trace-Flags registry: Bit 1 for Loopback (L-bit) and Bit 2 for Active (A-bit). This document is the reference for both. Bit 0, the Overflow bit, was allocated earlier by RFC 9197.
sections.eli5: The official list of switches on the packet got two new entries, so everyone agrees which switch is which.
